titre: A Planet That Theory Said Was Impossible
accroche: On October 6, 1995, in Florence, two astronomers announce a giant planet four days from its star, something theory forbade.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 6, 1995, at a conference in Florence, Michel Mayor announces the discovery of a planet orbiting 51 Pegasi, a Sun-like star fifty light-years from Earth. The room is skeptical. What Mayor describes should not, according to the theory of the day, exist.

## A wobbling star

Neither he nor his doctoral student Didier Queloz has seen the planet: no telescope of the time is capable of it. What they measure is the motion of the star itself. An orbiting planet does not circle alone; it tugs on its star, which in turn traces a tiny circle around the common center of mass. This motion, too faint to be seen, can be read in the light: when the star moves slightly away from Earth, its spectrum shifts toward the red; when it approaches, toward the blue. This is the radial velocity method.

With the Élodie spectrograph at the Haute-Provence Observatory, Mayor and Queloz monitor 142 stars. The one in 51 Pegasi oscillates in a cycle that repeats every 4.2 days, far too fast for a system like ours, where Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun, already takes eighty-eight days to go around it.

## What theory forbade

The amplitude of the signal indicates a planet of about half the mass of Jupiter, a gas giant. But in the planetary formation models of the time, a gas giant can only form beyond a certain distance from its star, where ices can condense. A Jupiter four days from its star, closer to it than Mercury is to the Sun, has nowhere to have been born.

The discovery holds despite the initial objections. It forces a revision: these planets, since called “hot Jupiters,” form far from their star, then migrate inward through their interaction with the disk of gas and dust they come from. Planetary migration becomes a chapter in its own right in the theory of how systems form.

51 Pegasi b remains the first confirmed exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star; others had already been spotted, in 1992, but around a pulsar, a dead star, unfit to harbor life. Mayor and Queloz receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019. Since their discovery, more than 5,000 exoplanets have been confirmed, and neither of the two has ever needed to see a planet again to prove it exists: all it takes is watching its star tremble.

repere.texte: 51 Pegasi b orbits in 4.2 days, at about 7.8 million kilometers from its star, a little over 13 percent of the distance between Mercury and the Sun, with an estimated mass of about half that of Jupiter: the first “hot Jupiter” ever confirmed.
repere.source: Mayor, M. & Queloz, D., “A Jupiter-mass companion to a solar-type star,” Nature, vol. 378, 1995

carte.punch: A planet discovered without ever being seen: all it took was watching its star tremble.
carte.idee: In 1995, Mayor and Queloz do not see a planet around 51 Pegasi: they measure the tiny back-and-forth motion of its star, caused by the planet pulling it along in orbit. A signal so fast that it pointed to a gas giant hugging its star, something theory judged impossible.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Press release for the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Awarded to Mayor and Queloz for the discovery of 51 Pegasi b.

quiz.question: Why did the discovery of 51 Pegasi b seem impossible to astronomers at first?
choix: Because no instrument of the time could measure the motion of a star
Because the radial velocity method had never been tested before 1995
Because a gas giant should not be able to form so close to its star
Because 51 Pegasi is too young a star to host a planet
quiz.explication: The planetary formation models of the time placed gas giants far from their star, where ices condense. A Jupiter four days from its star, closer to it than Mercury is to the Sun, fit no known scenario, until it was understood that these planets migrate after they form. The radial velocity method, for its part, was already proven before 1995, and nothing points to a problem with the star's age.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many stars were Mayor and Queloz monitoring with the Élodie spectrograph?
choix: Twelve stars, chosen for their proximity to the Sun
Fifty stars, selected at random from the Hipparcos catalog
More than 5,000 stars, as part of an automated survey
quiz_supplementaire.explication: With the Élodie spectrograph at the Haute-Provence Observatory, Mayor and Queloz were monitoring 142 stars, including 51 Pegasi.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why don't the planets discovered around a pulsar in 1992 count as the first confirmed exoplanet around a Sun-like star?
choix: Because a pulsar is a dead star, unfit to harbor life, unlike a star such as the Sun
Because their existence was never confirmed by a second independent team
Because these planets orbited too far from their star to qualify as exoplanets
Because the 1992 discovery was published only after the 1995 one
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that other exoplanets had already been spotted in 1992, but around a pulsar, a dead star, which sets 51 Pegasi b apart as the first confirmed around a Sun-like star.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz receive in 2019?
choix: The Fields Medal, for their work in mathematics applied to astronomy
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry, for the spectral analysis of the atmosphere of 51 Pegasi b
The Royal Society's Copley Medal, for their careers as a whole
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mayor and Queloz receive the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019 for their discovery of 51 Pegasi b, the first confirmed exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star.
